advice.title: Fever: care at home and when to come back
advice.text: Give plenty of fluids and keep feeding or breastfeeding. Give fever medicine only as prescribed for the child's weight. advice.title: Breastfeeding and complementary feeding

advice.title: When to come back at once
advice.text: Come back the same day if your sight gets worse, the eye becomes more painful or red, light starts to hurt your eyes, or you notice new floaters, flashes of light or a shadow spreading across your vision. Any sudden loss of sight needs to be seen the same day, even if it recovers.

advice.title: Red eye: stopping the spread
advice.text: Wash your hands often, use your own towel and pillow, and avoid close contact with others for 10 to 14 days while the eye is red and watery. Do not put steroid drops, leftover drops or home remedies in the eye unless your eye doctor has advised them.

advice.title: Diabetes and your eyes
advice.text: If you have diabetes, have a dilated eye examination at least once a year, even when you see well, because early damage gives no symptoms and early treatment works best. Keeping blood sugar and blood pressure under control lowers the risk of losing sight.

advice.title: Protecting your eyes
advice.text: Wear protective glasses for farm work, grinding, welding and sport, and keep children away from firecrackers. Stopping smoking lowers the risk of cataract and macular disease. Have eye problems checked by a trained eye doctor rather than using remedies from untrained providers.

advice.title: Caring for your ears
advice.text: Do not put cotton buds, hairpins, oil or home remedies into the ears; wax usually comes out by itself. Keep dirty water out of the ears when bathing or swimming. See a doctor soon for ear pain, discharge, bleeding or hearing loss, and on the same day if hearing is lost suddenly.

advice.title: Protecting your hearing
advice.text: Keep phone and earphone volume below 60% of maximum, limit listening time and take breaks from loud sound. Use ear plugs or ear muffs in noisy work and at loud events, and keep away from loudspeakers.

advice.title: Nosebleed first aid
advice.text: If your nose bleeds, stay calm, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for at least 5 minutes; if it slows, keep holding for a full 15 minutes. Avoid picking the nose or blowing it hard, and keep the inside moist with saline spray or gel. Do not stop a blood thinner without asking the doctor who prescribed it. Go to the emergency department if bleeding is heavy or will not stop, or if you feel weak or faint.

advice.title: Tobacco and warning signs
advice.text: Stop all forms of tobacco, including cigarettes, bidis, gutkha, khaini and tobacco paan, stop chewing areca nut (supari), and cut down alcohol. See a doctor if a mouth ulcer has not healed in 3 weeks, or if you notice a red or white patch in the mouth, a lump in the neck, or a hoarse voice that does not go away.

advice.title: Serious drug reaction: warning signs
advice.text: Come to hospital at once if you get fever with a sore throat or sore red eyes, a painful red or purple rash, blisters or peeling skin, or sores in the mouth, eyes or genitals. If a medicine caused your skin reaction, keep a record of its name, tell every doctor and pharmacist, and do not start any new medicine, even one bought without a prescription, before asking your doctor.

advice.title: Leprosy: treatment and self-care
advice.text: Leprosy is curable. Take the multidrug treatment regularly until the full course is finished. If your hands or feet are numb, check them every day for cuts, burns, blisters or red spots, soak dry skin in water and then apply oil or moisturiser, and wear footwear with a soft inner sole. Come back at once if patches become red and swollen, or you get nerve pain, new numbness or weakness, painful lumps with fever, or red eyes.

advice.title: Fungal skin infection (ringworm)
advice.text: Use the antifungal medicine regularly and continue it as advised, usually for 2 weeks after the rash clears. Do not apply steroid or mixed creams bought without a prescription. Wear loose clothes and change them when sweaty, do not share towels, bed linen or clothes, wash undergarments and socks often and dry them in the sun, and get family members with a similar rash examined.

advice.title: Scabies: treat everyone together
advice.text: Everyone in the household and other close contacts must be treated at the same time, even if they do not itch. Wash clothes, towels and bed linen when you start treatment, and seal anything that cannot be washed in a bag for 3 days. Itching often carries on for a few weeks after the mites are killed.

advice.title: Help in a crisis

advice.title: Keeping the home safe
advice.text: Ask a family member to lock away all medicines, pesticides, acids and other poisons, and to remove anything else you might use to harm yourself. Share your safety plan with them so they know your warning signs and whom to call.

advice.title: Taking antidepressants
advice.text: Antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start working and up to 6 weeks for the full effect, so take them every day even if you notice no change at first. Do not stop them suddenly, and do not take extra to make up for a missed dose. Carry on for as long as your doctor advises, usually at least six months after you feel better. Tell your doctor straight away about troublesome side effects or any thoughts of harming yourself, and ask before drinking alcohol or driving.

advice.title: Daily care of teeth and gums
advice.text: Brush your teeth twice a day for at least two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste. Cut down sweets, sugary snacks and fizzy drinks, especially between meals, and drink water instead. Have your mouth checked by a dentist regularly.

advice.title: Tobacco, areca nut and mouth cancer
advice.text: Stop all tobacco, smoked or chewed (bidi, cigarettes, gutka, khaini), and areca nut (supari, paan). Tobacco damages the gums, and tobacco and areca nut are leading causes of mouth cancer; ask us for help to quit. Look inside your mouth regularly, and see a dentist or doctor without delay if an ulcer or a white or red patch has not healed in 2 weeks. Do not put tobacco or anything else on it.

advice.title: Toothache and swelling
advice.text: Until your treatment, keep the area clean and rinse with warm salt water. Do not put tobacco, camphor, salt, balm or heat on the tooth or the swollen cheek, and take only the medicines prescribed for you. Go to the hospital emergency department at once if the swelling spreads, or you have fever or difficulty opening your mouth, swallowing or breathing.

advice.title: After a tooth extraction
advice.text: If the socket bleeds, place a rolled, damp gauze or clean cotton pad over it and bite firmly for 20 minutes. For the next 24 hours avoid smoking, alcohol and exercise, keep your head raised and do not disturb the clot. If bleeding continues after a second 20 minutes of pressure, come to the hospital straight away; if you take blood-thinning medicine, come as soon as bleeding fails to stop or starts again.

advice.text: If you smoke, stopping for several weeks before the operation makes your anaesthetic safer, and do not smoke on the day of the operation. advice.title: Chest pain: when to call an ambulance
advice.text: Call an ambulance or come to the emergency department at once if you get chest pain, pressure or tightness that lasts more than 15 minutes, spreads to your arm, jaw, neck or back, or comes with sweating, feeling sick, breathlessness or fainting. Do not drive yourself.

advice.title: Looking after yourself with heart failure
advice.text: Weigh yourself every morning after passing urine and before breakfast, and write it down. Contact us quickly if your weight goes up over a few days, your feet or legs swell more, you get more breathless, or you cannot lie flat. Avoid very salty foods such as pickles, papad and packaged snacks, and do not use salt substitutes unless your doctor agrees. Take your heart medicines every day and stay as active as you comfortably can.

advice.title: Protecting your heart after a heart attack
advice.text: Join the cardiac rehabilitation programme if it is offered. Build up to 20 to 30 minutes of activity every day, enough to make you slightly breathless. Eat more fruit, vegetables, whole grains, pulses and fish, and cook with plant oils rather than ghee or butter. Stop smoking completely, keep alcohol low, and keep taking your heart medicines; do not stop them without talking to your doctor.

advice.title: If you take a blood thinner
advice.text: Take your blood thinner at the same time every day and do not stop it unless your doctor tells you to. Tell every doctor, dentist and pharmacist that you take it. Come to hospital at once if you have black stools, vomit blood, pass blood in your urine, get a severe headache, or suddenly have weakness of the face, arm or leg or difficulty speaking.

advice.text: Call an ambulance or come to hospital at once if you or someone with you suddenly gets weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, difficulty speaking or understanding, loss of vision, or loss of balance. advice.title: Living safely with seizures
advice.text: Do not drive until your doctor tells you it is safe and the law allows it. Take a shower rather than a bath, do not swim alone, avoid working at heights, and take care when cooking. Take your seizure medicines every day and do not stop them suddenly. Sleep well and avoid alcohol binges.

advice.title: First aid for a seizure (for family)
advice.text: Stay calm, move hard objects away and cushion the head. Do not put anything in the mouth or hold the person down. When the jerking stops, turn them on their side. Time the seizure, and call an ambulance if it lasts 5 minutes or more, another seizure follows, they are injured, or breathing is difficult.

advice.title: Headache: when to come at once
advice.text: Come to hospital at once for a sudden, very severe headache, a headache with fever and a stiff neck, fits, confusion or weakness, or a headache after a head injury. Keep a headache diary, and avoid taking painkillers on many days each month, as this can make headaches worse.

advice.title: Looking after your kidneys
advice.text: Keep active, aiming for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week if you are able. Do not smoke or chew tobacco. Keep salt below 5 g a day (about one level teaspoon in total), and cut down pickles, papads and packaged foods. Eat more vegetables and pulses. Do not take painkillers bought from a shop, or herbal or traditional remedies, without asking your doctor, as some can harm the kidneys.

advice.title: Preventing kidney stones
advice.text: Drink enough fluid, mostly water, spread through the day to pass about 2 to 2.5 litres of urine a day; drink more in hot weather or when you sweat a lot. Keep salt to 4 to 5 g a day and do not eat large amounts of meat, fish or eggs. Do not cut out milk and curd: a normal amount of calcium in the diet is advised. Keep a healthy weight and cut down sugary drinks and alcohol.

advice.title: Helping urinary symptoms
advice.text: Drink less in the evening and before going out, but do not cut your total fluids too much. Cut down tea, coffee and alcohol. Take your time and try passing urine a second time before leaving the toilet. When you get a sudden urge, try to hold on a little longer to train your bladder. Keep your bowels regular and tell your doctor about all the medicines you take.

advice.title: Kidney and urine warning signs
advice.text: Come to hospital at once if you cannot pass urine or pass very little, pass blood clots, have fever with shivering and pain in the side or back, have severe pain with vomiting, feel very weak or have palpitations, or become breathless. If you are on dialysis, also come at once if the fistula stops buzzing or the PD fluid turns cloudy.

advice.title: Caring for your feet
advice.text: Look at both feet every day, including between the toes, or ask someone to help. Do not walk barefoot, in socks only or in thin slippers, at home or outside. Feel inside your shoes before wearing them. Wash your feet daily in water that is not hot and dry well between the toes. Do not warm your feet with a heater or hot-water bottle. Do not cut corns yourself or use corn plasters. Use moisturiser, but not between the toes, and cut nails straight across. Show a doctor at once any blister, cut, scratch or sore.

advice.title: Low sugar (hypoglycaemia)
advice.text: If you feel shaky, sweaty, confused or suddenly hungry, check your sugar if you can and take glucose or sugar dissolved in water at once. Check again after 15 minutes and repeat if still low, then eat a snack or meal. Teach your family what to do. Tell your doctor about every low, and come at once if you needed help from someone or became unconscious.

advice.title: When you are unwell (sick-day rules)
advice.text: When you have fever, vomiting, diarrhoea or cannot eat, never stop your insulin. Check your sugar more often, and ketones if you have been told how. Drink plenty of fluids and ask your doctor which tablets to pause while unwell. Come to hospital at once if you keep vomiting or cannot keep fluids down, have abdominal pain, fast deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion, or your sugar stays very high.

advice.title: Thyroid treatment and tests
advice.text: Take your thyroid medicine every day as prescribed, even when you feel well. After a dose change it can take several weeks to months for symptoms to settle, so keep your blood test appointments. Tell your doctor if you take biotin (often in hair, skin and nail supplements), as it can make thyroid blood tests wrong.

advice.title: Indigestion and acidity
advice.text: Eat healthy, regular meals, lose weight if you are overweight and stop smoking. Avoid things that bring on your symptoms, such as alcohol, coffee, chocolate and fatty food. Have your main meal at least 3 hours before going to bed, and raise the head end of your bed.

advice.title: Looking after your liver
advice.text: Stop alcohol completely. If you have fluid in the abdomen, do not add salt at the table and avoid pickles, papads and ready-made or packaged foods, but do not stop salt completely. advice.title: Staying safe on DMARD medicines
advice.text: Have your blood tests done on the dates given and bring your monitoring record to every visit. Contact the clinic at once if you get a sore throat, fever or other infection, mouth ulcers, unexplained bruising or bleeding, yellow eyes, or a new cough or breathlessness. Do not start or stop any medicine, including herbal remedies, without asking, and tell us before planning a pregnancy.

advice.title: Living with gout
advice.text: Take the urate-lowering tablets every day, even when you have no pain. Attacks can happen more often in the first few months; this does not mean the medicine is failing, so do not stop it. Cut down on alcohol, especially beer, on sugary drinks, and on red meat and seafood, and lose weight if you are overweight.

advice.title: When to come at once
advice.text: Come to hospital the same day if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with fever or if you take medicines that lower immunity. If you are over 50 and get a new headache, pain in the jaw when chewing, a tender scalp, or any loss or blurring of vision or double vision, come at once: this can cause blindness if not treated quickly.

advice.text: Do the balance and strength exercises you have been shown, regularly. advice.title: After a fall

advice.text: Take the regular pain medicine at the times written, even when the pain is less, and use the extra (breakthrough) dose when pain comes through, as explained. advice.title: When to contact the team at once

advice.title: The last days of life: advice for family
advice.text: In the last days of life it is usual to sleep more, eat and drink less, and for breathing to become shallow, irregular or noisy. Keep the mouth and lips moist, turn gently, and call the team if there is pain, distress or restlessness. Keep the team's phone number where everyone can find it.

advice.text: Stop tobacco in every form, including gutka and khaini, and avoid alcohol. Be physically active for at least 150 minutes a week, for example 30 minutes a day on 5 days. advice.text: Eat about a quarter more food than usual, including a variety of foods, and use iodised salt. Rest for 2 hours in the day and 8 hours at night. Take the iron-folic acid and calcium tablets exactly as prescribed. Attend every antenatal check-up and plan your delivery in a hospital.

advice.title: Danger signs in pregnancy
advice.text: Go to the nearest hospital at once if you have bleeding, high fever, severe tiredness or breathlessness, headache with blurred vision, fits or swelling all over the body, leaking of water, labour pains before time or for more than 12 hours, or if the baby moves less than usual.

la-doses.verified: Read on 2026-09-25 from the full-text PDF of the article (the publisher page and the BNF site both returned HTTP 403, so the BNF could not be checked directly). mgPerKg and strengths: Table 1, Commonly used preparations of local anaesthetics: lidocaine 3 mg/kg at 1% and 2%; lidocaine with adrenaline 6 mg/kg at 1% and 2%; prilocaine 6 mg/kg and with adrenaline 8 mg/kg at 1% and 2%; bupivacaine 2 mg/kg and with adrenaline 2.5 mg/kg at 0.25% and 0.5%; ropivacaine 3 mg/kg and with adrenaline 4 mg/kg at 0.75% (the only ropivacaine strength in the table). Each row was checked against the table's dosage factor column (maximum dose divided by concentration, e.g. lidocaine 1% 0.3 mL/kg = 3 mg/kg). maxMg: the Discussion quotes the BNF 63rd edition maxima lidocaine 200 mg, bupivacaine 150 mg and prilocaine 400 mg and pairs them with 67, 75 and 67 kg, i.e. the plain mg/kg doses, so they are entered as plain-solution ceilings only. The source gives no mg ceiling for solutions with adrenaline or for ropivacaine, so those are null. Levobupivacaine is not in this source and is left out. Body weight rule and mixture rule in notes are from the section Instructions for use and the Discussion.
notes: Use ideal body weight, and use 70 kg for anyone weighing 70 kg or more: the source and the BNF base these doses on ideal body weight. This matters most where no mg ceiling is given (with adrenaline, and ropivacaine).
Mixtures: calculate as if the whole volume were the agent with the greater toxic potential.
Toxicity varies with each patient's pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, so a dose within the maximum can still cause toxicity.
If toxicity is suspected, stop injecting and follow the local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) protocol.

frequency: Each time column is one clock hour; record the actual time of every observation.
Supportive care (companion, pain relief, oral fluid, posture): record every hour.

Baseline FHR and decelerations: every 30 minutes in the first stage and every 5 minutes in the second stage; in the second stage record the most clinically significant value within each 15 minute timeframe.
Amniotic fluid, fetal position, caput and moulding: at each vaginal examination, every 4 hours unless otherwise indicated.
Pulse, blood pressure and temperature: every 4 hours; urine protein and acetone every 4 hours or each time the woman voids.
Contractions (frequency and duration): every 30 minutes in the first stage and at least every 15 minutes in the second stage.
Cervix: every 4 hours in the first stage unless otherwise indicated. Descent: every 4 hours before the vaginal examination, and plot at every vaginal examination.
Oxytocin: when used, record the amount being given every 60 minutes.
notes: Start the LCG when the woman enters the active first stage (cervix 5 cm or more), whatever her parity or membrane status; do not start it in the latent phase.

At every assessment follow Assess, Record, Check against the Alert column, Plan. Circle any alert value, alert the senior midwife or doctor, and record the assessment and the plan agreed with the woman in the shared decision-making section.

Cervix alert: dilatation stays at the same value for the listed hours or more with no progress. Second stage alert: birth not completed 3 hours (nulliparous) or 2 hours (multiparous) from the start of the active second stage. In the second stage, mark P when pushing begins.
If contractions are 2 or fewer or more than 5 per 10 minutes, or last under 20 or over 60 seconds, recount over another 10 minutes before alerting.

Alert thresholds are early-warning signals, not diagnoses. Decide on the overall assessment of the woman and baby rather than one observation; they do not replace clinical judgement or local guidelines.
If labour lasts beyond 12 hours, continue on a new LCG.

tips: One condition per line, with disease names written in full and no abbreviations.
Line (a) is the disease, injury or complication that directly caused death, never a mode of dying such as heart failure, respiratory failure or cardiac arrest.
Each line is due to the condition on the line below it; the underlying cause, which started the sequence, goes on the lowest used line of Part I.
Give the approximate interval between onset and death for every condition, e.g. from birth, several years or unknown.
Part II holds other conditions that contributed but were not part of the sequence. Old age or senility goes only in Part II, and never when a more specific cause is known.
For injury or poisoning, state the nature of the injury and the external cause; if accident, suicide or homicide is not yet known, still fill in the cause and mark the manner Pending investigation.

actEarly: Developmental milestones are things most children (75% or more) can do by a certain age.
You know your child best. Don't wait. If your child is not meeting one or more milestones, has lost skills he or she once had, or you have other concerns, act early.
Talk with your child's doctor, share your concerns, and ask about developmental screening.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children be screened for general development using standardized, validated tools at 9, 18, and 30 months and for autism at 18 and 24 months or whenever a parent or provider has a concern.
If you or the doctor are still concerned, ask for a referral to a specialist who can evaluate your child more.
If you or the doctor are still concerned, call your state or territory's early intervention program to find out if your child can get services to help.
Learn the Signs. Act Early. materials are not a substitute for standardized, validated developmental screening tools.

conditions.label: Tuberculosis
conditions.report: Notify every TB case (microbiologically confirmed, or clinically diagnosed and started on treatment) on Ni-kshay or to the district TB notification nodal officer, at diagnosis or at the start of treatment. Notification is mandatory for public and private providers, and non-notification is punishable under the 2018 gazette notification.

conditions.label: Acute diarrhoeal disease (including acute gastroenteritis)
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP portal on the P form (presumptive case, entered by the treating doctor or facility). Tell the District Surveillance Officer about any cluster or unusual rise in cases so that the rapid response team can investigate.

conditions.label: Cholera
conditions.report: Report as acute diarrhoeal disease on the IHIP P form; a laboratory-confirmed case is reported by the laboratory on the L form. Tell the District Surveillance Officer about any cluster so that the rapid response team can investigate.

conditions.label: Bacillary dysentery
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed Shigella dysentery on the L form.

conditions.label: Acute viral hepatitis
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed hepatitis A and hepatitis E on the L form. Tell the District Surveillance Officer about any cluster.

conditions.label: Enteric (typhoid) fever
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed typhoid on the L form.

conditions.label: Malaria
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed cases (P. vivax and P. falciparum) on the L form.

conditions.label: Dengue
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form (dengue, DHF or DSS); the laboratory reports confirmed dengue on the L form. Tell the District Surveillance Officer about any cluster.

conditions.label: Chikungunya
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed chikungunya on the L form.

conditions.label: Acute encephalitis syndrome (including Japanese encephalitis)
conditions.report: Report as acute encephalitis syndrome on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed Japanese encephalitis on the L form.

conditions.label: Meningitis
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed meningococcal meningitis on the L form.

conditions.label: Measles and rubella (fever with rash)
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form, and notify every case of fever with maculopapular rash to the District Immunization Officer or WHO NPSN surveillance medical officer for case-based measles-rubella surveillance and investigation.

conditions.label: Diphtheria
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form, and notify the District Immunization Officer or WHO NPSN surveillance medical officer for case-based vaccine-preventable disease surveillance; the laboratory reports confirmed cases on the L form.

conditions.label: Pertussis (whooping cough)
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form, and notify the District Immunization Officer or WHO NPSN surveillance medical officer for case-based vaccine-preventable disease surveillance.

conditions.label: Neonatal tetanus
conditions.report: Notify the District Immunization Officer or WHO NPSN surveillance medical officer for case-based vaccine-preventable disease surveillance and investigation.

conditions.label: Acute flaccid paralysis (under 15 years)
conditions.report: In a child under 15 years, report every case of acute flaccid paralysis promptly to the District Immunization Officer or WHO NPSN surveillance medical officer for case-based polio surveillance, and on the IHIP P form.

conditions.label: Chickenpox
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form. Tell the District Surveillance Officer about any cluster.

conditions.label: Fever of unknown origin (PUO)
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form as fever of unknown origin until a specific diagnosis is made.

conditions.label: Acute respiratory infection or influenza-like illness
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form (ARI or ILI). Tell the District Surveillance Officer about any cluster or unusual rise.

conditions.label: Pneumonia
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form.

conditions.label: Leptospirosis
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form; the laboratory reports confirmed leptospirosis on the L form.

conditions.label: Dog or other animal bite, and human rabies
conditions.report: Report dog bites on the IHIP P form. Suspected human rabies cases and deaths are also reported on IDSP-IHIP, and human rabies is a notifiable disease in most states (23 states and UTs in 2025).

conditions.label: Snakebite
conditions.report: Report on the IHIP P form (snake bite). MoHFW asked all states in November 2024 to make snakebite cases and deaths notifiable, so report every suspected or probable case and every death.

conditions.label: Heatstroke
conditions.report: Include every heatstroke case and death in the facility's daily report on IHIP under the National Heat-Related Illness and Death Surveillance, which runs from 1 March in the heat season for facilities from PHC upwards.
